summary: The legal domain produces at most 29 output bits, so runtime tiers cannot separate logarithmic and mildly superlinear bit-processing reliably. The required output length supplies a matching lower bound that directly certifies the current solution's optimality.

optimality.argument: For q greater than one, the returned encoding contains exactly floor(log2(q)) characters, so materializing the required string takes Omega(log q) time in the worst case. The current solution converts q to its binary representation once and takes one linear-length slice, giving O(log q) time. For q = 1, both the input and the empty result require constant work, consistent with the bound over the complete domain.

replacement_checks.evidence: The contract requires exactly floor(log2(q)) returned bits for q greater than one, and every character of that output must be materialized.
Python constructs the binary representation of q once, then the solution slices its O(log q)-character representation once.

Independent exhaustive verification covered every num from 0 through 1,000,000, deterministic randomized verification covered 50,000 legal inputs including group boundaries and the maximum, and all ten visible correctness cases passed the independent oracle and both protected sources.
